questions.q: Where do you start when organising a club shoot?

options.text: By buying the trophies
By publishing the results
By agreeing terms with the ground

questions.explain: First come the venue, the terms, the permits and safety.

questions.q: Who designs the layouts of an international Sporting™ competition?

options.text: The course designer
The spectators
Each shooter for themselves

questions.explain: In Sporting™ the course designer prepares the layouts, and officials check them before the start. In Compak® Sporting the jury can instead pick ready-made setting tables.

questions.q: Where may shooters practise on the competition trajectories before the event?

options.text: In Sporting™, on the competition layouts
In Compak® Sporting, with the targets combined differently
In neither discipline

questions.explain: In Sporting™ nobody may practise on the competition layouts. In Compak® Sporting practice is allowed, but with a different setting table, so the targets are combined differently.

questions.q: Can someone who does not shoot help at a competition?

options.text: No, only shooters may help
Only as a certified referee
Yes, as a volunteer: registration, photos and more

questions.explain: Volunteers are needed at nearly all competitions, and many of them do not shoot.

questions.q: How many targets does an international FITASC competition usually have?
questions.explain: An international competition is usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25.

questions.q: Who usually sets the format of a club shoot?

options.text: The shooters, on the day
The referee at the first stand
The organiser, in the programme

questions.explain: The organiser sets the number of targets and the format of a club shoot, and the programme says what they are.

questions.q: Why do continental and world Compak® Sporting championships use new machines?

options.text: So that conditions are equal for everyone
Because old machines are banned by law
So that the targets fly faster

questions.explain: The host club may not use the machines it normally shoots on: 48 new machines are set up for the championship alone.

questions.q: Which special Sporting™ format is allowed only at Grand Prix events?

options.text: Squads of ten shooters on one stand
A line of 3 stands with 5 traps each
Rounds of 50 targets on one layout

questions.explain: A line of 3 shooting stands with 5 traps each is allowed for Grand Prix events only.

questions.q: What happens if you come to the stand without hearing protection or safety glasses?

options.text: You may shoot, but you get a warning
You are treated as absent and may not shoot
The referee gives you a spare set

questions.explain: In both disciplines a shooter without hearing protection or safety glasses is treated as absent, and the lateness rules apply.

questions.q: Where may you check that your gun works?

options.text: On the first competition stand, before the round
Anywhere on the ground, if the area is clear
At a special test stand, if the ground has one

questions.explain: Test shots on a competition stand are not allowed in either discipline; use the test stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, a shooter arrives after the first shooter has called for the first target. What happens?

options.text: Nothing, he joins in
He gets 25 zeros for that round
He shoots the round alone later without penalty
He loses one target

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting shot by squad, arriving after the first call costs 25 zeros for the round. For a reason outside your control, you can appeal to the jury in writing on the same day.

questions.q: What is the largest number of shooters in a squad?
questions.explain: In both Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting a squad has at most 6 shooters.

questions.q: Two shooters tie for 5th place. How are they ranked?

options.text: By a 25-target shoot-off for that place
By drawing lots after the event has ended
They share it; countback from the 8th layout or Compak sets the order
By age, with the younger shooter placed higher

questions.explain: Shoot-offs are only for the top three. Below that, tied shooters share the place, and countback compares the 8th layout or Compak, then the 7th, and so on.

questions.q: In Compak in line, when do you count as late?

options.text: When your number is cancelled in the system and the next shooter is on station 1
As soon as the referee has called out your name for the first time
Only after the whole group has finished shooting the round

questions.explain: Both things must have happened: your number is already cancelled in the computer system, and the next shooter stands on station 1. The penalty is 25 zeros for the round.

questions.q: How do you carry your gun between stands?

options.text: Open, so everyone can see it is not loaded, and without a sling
Closed and unloaded, on a sling over your shoulder
Closed, with the safety catch on, pointing at the ground

questions.explain: Guns are carried open and slings are not allowed; a semi-automatic is carried with its breech open.

questions.q: How does a category differ from a class?

options.text: They mean the same thing in the rules
A category is by results, a class by age
A category is by age or sex, a class by results

questions.explain: Junior, Lady, Senior and Veteran are categories by age or sex; AA, A, B and C are national classes by average score.

questions.q: How are tied shooters below third place ranked?

options.text: They share it; countback from the 8th layout sets the order
By a shoot-off of 25 targets for the place
By drawing lots after the event has ended

questions.explain: There are no shoot-offs below third place: the place is shared and countback sets the order, from the 8th layout or Compak back to the 1st.

questions.q: A shooter born in 1971 enters a FITASC competition in 2027. Which category?

options.text: Men
Senior
Veteran
Master

questions.explain: He turns 56 in 2027, so he is Senior from 1 January, whatever his birthday.

questions.q: How many targets are in the first round of a shoot-off?
questions.explain: A shoot-off is a round of 25 targets; if the scores are still level, sudden death follows.

questions.q: Two shooters tie for 7th place. What happens?

options.text: A 25-target shoot-off
Sudden death at once
A coin toss by the jury
They share the place and are ordered by countback

questions.explain: Shoot-offs are only for places 1–3; below that, tied shooters are listed by countback from the eighth layout or Compak.

questions.q: From what age can women and girls enter the Lady category under FITASC rules?

options.text: From 1 January of the year they turn 13
From the day of their 18th birthday
From 1 January of the year they turn 21

questions.explain: Lady starts from the year of the 13th birthday, counted by year of birth.

questions.q: Does the Lady category have an upper age limit?

options.text: Yes, it ends at the age of 55
No, the FITASC table sets none
Yes, it ends at the age of 40

questions.explain: The FITASC table sets no upper limit for Lady.

questions.q: Do women shoot shorter or easier trajectories?

options.text: Yes, the trajectories are shorter
Only in Compak® Sporting events
No, the targets are the same for all

questions.explain: The category affects only the ranking, not the targets.

questions.q: How should you translate the FITASC category “Senior” for a client?

options.text: “Adults”
“Experienced shooters”
“Top class”
“The 56–65 age group”

questions.explain: In FITASC Senior is an age group of 56–65; the main adult category is Men.

questions.q: How many shooters are in a Men team in Sporting™?

options.text: Four
Three
Six
Five

questions.explain: Teams usually have three shooters, but the Men team in Sporting™ has four.

questions.q: Which shorts are allowed at FITASC competitions?

options.text: Any sports shorts
No shorts at all
Long ones, near the knee

questions.explain: Short shorts are banned; long ones are allowed if they end no more than 5 cm above the knee.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold on the stand?

options.text: One
Two at most
Three at most
As many as fit

questions.explain: Both rulebooks limit a semi-automatic to no more than two cartridges.

questions.q: Are gun slings allowed in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: No, in neither discipline
Yes, only in Compak® Sporting
Only between stations

questions.explain: Slings and straps are banned in both disciplines; guns are carried open.

questions.q: A shooter arrives on the stand without safety glasses. What happens?

options.text: Only a warning
Allowed with ear protection on
Treated as absent

questions.explain: Glasses and ear protection are compulsory; without them the shooter may not shoot.

questions.q: Why are sandals banned?

options.text: For safety reasons
Because they are unfashionable
They are not banned

questions.explain: Closed shoes protect the feet, so sandals are banned.

questions.q: Where is the competitor number worn?

options.text: On the left sleeve
On the front of the cap
On the back

questions.explain: The number is worn on your back, anywhere from the shoulders down to the waist, and nothing may hide any part of it.

questions.q: You are an interpreter standing near the stand. Must you wear ear protection?

options.text: No, only the shooters on the stand
Only during finals and shoot-offs
Yes, everyone on or near a layout
Only if the referee asks you to

questions.explain: Hearing protection is compulsory for shooters, referees, staff and spectators.

questions.q: Which footwear is banned in both disciplines?

options.text: Trail shoes
Sandals
Boots
Trainers

questions.explain: Sandals are forbidden for safety reasons.

questions.q: A shooter comes to the station in sandals for a practice round. Is it allowed?

options.text: Yes, in practice only
No, not in practice either
Yes, with socks
Only with the referee's permission

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting dress code bans sandals for safety, in practice and in competition.

questions.q: Does a spectator need hearing protection?

options.text: No, only the people who are shooting
Yes, the rules require it near the layout
Only at championships, not at club shoots

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

questions.q: May you take photos with flash?

options.text: Yes, if you stay in the spectator area
Only once the referee has agreed
No, because flash can dazzle the shooter

questions.explain: Flash distracts and dazzles the shooter, so spectators do not use it.

questions.q: What happens if a spectator coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: The shooter can get a yellow card; the adviser is sent away
Nothing at all, as long as the advice is given quietly
The shooter must shoot the whole stand again from the start

questions.explain: Advice during a competition counts as coaching, which both rulebooks forbid.

questions.q: When is it right to applaud?

options.text: While the shooter is aiming at the target
After the stand, when nobody is about to call
Just before the shooter calls “pull”

questions.explain: While anyone on the layout is shooting or about to call, spectators stay quiet; applause comes when the shooter has finished.

questions.q: Where may a spectator stand?

options.text: In front of the firing line, for a better view
Next to the traps, out of the line of fire
In the spectator area, behind the stand

questions.explain: Spectators stand in the area set aside for them, usually behind the stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, a spectator loudly criticises a ruling. How do the rules see this?

options.text: As an attempt to influence the referee
As normal support from the crowd
As a breach of the dress code

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the rules count open criticism of a decision by shooters or spectators, without the referee’s permission, as an attempt to influence.

questions.q: What do you need to film a competition with a drone?

options.text: Nothing, as long as it flies above the stands
The organiser’s permission, plus the country’s drone rules
Permission from one of the shooters in the squad

questions.explain: Flying over a shooting ground needs the organiser’s permission, and the drone rules of the country always apply.

questions.q: Where should the coach be while a child is shooting in a training session?

options.text: Behind the squad, where he can watch the whole stand
Right beside the child, able to take the gun at once
At the trap, ready to stop the targets

questions.explain: In training, direct supervision means the coach stands next to the child and can step in at once. In a competition the referee runs the stand.

questions.q: Your daughter only comes to watch a competition. Does she need hearing protection?

options.text: Yes, the rules require it near the layout
No, only the people who are shooting need it
Only if she stands right next to the stand

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for spectators near the layout; in Sporting™ children outside the clubhouse wear it at all times.

questions.q: What should you do when a child gets tired during a session?

options.text: Add one more round to build character
Switch to a harder target to keep interest
Stop the session: tiredness lowers attention

questions.explain: When attention drops the risk of a gun-handling mistake rises, so it is better to stop.

questions.q: How are guns and cartridges usually stored at home?

options.text: In the gun slip under the bed, ready for training
In a cupboard the child can open, but unloaded
In a locked safe, cartridges apart, keys with adults

questions.explain: Store guns as the law of your country requires; usually a locked safe, cartridges separately, keys only with adults.

questions.q: What do you do with empty cases after a round?

options.text: Leave them where they fall
Put them in the bin provided
Kick them under the stand

questions.explain: Cases go in the bin where there is one, and semi-automatic users pick up their ejected cases.

questions.q: Where might a ground require steel shot?

options.text: Where the law restricts lead
Only at international championships
Only on very windy days

questions.explain: Lead rules depend on the country and the area, often near water; check in advance.

questions.q: What is special about biodegradable targets?

options.text: They are heavier than standard ones
They glow at dusk for visibility
They have no pitch and break down more easily

questions.explain: They are made without pitch, so they leave less of it in the soil.

questions.q: Which statement about practice before a competition is true?

options.text: In Sporting™ you may practise on the competition layouts
In Compak® Sporting you may not practise at all before the competition
In Sporting™ you may practise only on other parts of the ground

questions.explain: In Sporting™ the competition layouts are closed to practice, so you practise on other parts of the ground. In Compak® Sporting you may practise on the competition target flights under a different setting table; at championships, official practice opens on the Saturday before the championship.

questions.q: Why plan to arrive a day or two before the competition?

options.text: To settle in, adjust to local time and practise
To pay a smaller entry fee for arriving early
To choose your own squad and starting time

questions.explain: The body needs time after a long trip, and an early arrival lets you prepare calmly.

questions.q: In which time are the shooting times given?

options.text: In the time of your home country
In the local time at the venue
In UTC, the same in all countries

questions.explain: The schedule is in local time, so check your phone's clock after the flight.

questions.q: Who issues the European Firearms Pass?

options.text: FITASC, through your national federation
The organiser of the competition you enter
The office for firearms permits in the country where you live

questions.explain: You get the pass in the country where you live, from the office that handles firearms permits, if you lawfully own firearms.

questions.q: What most often proves the reason for a shooter's trip with a gun?

options.text: An invitation letter from the organiser
A return ticket for the same flight
A photo of you at the shooting ground

questions.explain: An invitation letter with your name, the event, the place and the dates is the usual proof.

questions.q: Which statement about the European Firearms Pass is true?

options.text: It replaces the gun laws of the country you visit
It lists the specific guns you may travel with
It stays valid with no time limit at all

questions.explain: Each gun must be entered in the pass, the pass has an expiry date, and local laws still apply.

questions.q: Who can get a European Firearms Pass?

options.text: Any tourist who visits a shooting ground
An EU resident who lawfully owns a gun
Only referees with a FITASC licence

questions.explain: The pass is issued to lawful gun owners in the country where they live: in the EU, and in Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

questions.q: What is usually needed to bring a gun into a country outside the EU?

options.text: Only the plane ticket and a gun case
A temporary import permit from that country
Nothing, if you have shot there before

questions.explain: Each country has its own rules, and a temporary permit is most often required.

questions.q: Why keep the customs declaration for the gun?

options.text: To sell the gun at the destination
To pay a lower fee on your next trip
To bring the gun back home without trouble

questions.explain: The declaration shows that it is the same gun you brought in and are taking out.

questions.q: What can you do if the permit will not be ready in time?

options.text: Hire a gun at the destination
Pack the gun in your suitcase anyway
Send the gun to the ground by post

questions.explain: Taking a gun without the permits is not allowed; hiring one at the ground is the lawful option.

questions.q: Where does the gun travel on a flight?

options.text: In the cabin, in an overhead locker
In hand luggage, in a soft gun slip
In checked baggage, in a hard case

questions.explain: Guns travel only in checked baggage, unloaded, in a lockable hard case.

questions.q: How do cartridges travel by plane?

options.text: In checked baggage, securely packed, with the airline's approval
In your hand luggage, so that security can check them
In your jacket pockets, to save baggage weight

questions.explain: The IATA rules allow cartridges only in checked baggage, securely packed and with the airline's approval, and airlines may be stricter.

questions.q: Where should you keep the gun documents during the flight?

options.text: In the gun case, with the gun
In your hand luggage, with you
In your checked suitcase

questions.explain: Documents may be needed at check-in, at the border and after landing, so keep them with you.

questions.q: What cartridge limit do the IATA rules usually allow a passenger?

options.text: No limit, if the cartridges are boxed
Up to 50 kg, shared with the group
Up to 5 kg gross, for your own use

questions.explain: Up to 5 kg gross per person is the IATA limit, but an airline may lower it or refuse cartridges.

questions.q: Why are competition cartridges usually bought at the destination?

options.text: Because FITASC asks for cartridges from the host
Because cartridges are always cheaper abroad
Because airlines allow only a few boxes

questions.explain: Baggage allows only a few kilograms of cartridges, and a competition needs hundreds of them.

questions.q: What is the most shot a cartridge may hold under the FITASC rules?

options.text: 28 g of lead, with a +2% tolerance
24 g of lead, with no tolerance
32 g of lead, with a +5% tolerance

questions.explain: In both disciplines the limit is 28 g of lead with a +2% tolerance.

questions.q: A ground allows steel shot only. What should you check?

options.text: Whether the shop sells reloaded cartridges
Whether your gun and chokes suit steel
Whether lead is still fine for practice

questions.explain: Steel shot does not suit all guns and chokes, so check in advance.

questions.q: After a flight a few time zones east (up to about 8), which light pattern helps the body clock adjust?

options.text: Bright light in the evening and dark mornings
Daylight in the morning and a dim evening
A dark room for the whole first day

questions.explain: After such a flight the body clock has to move earlier, and morning light helps it do that. For very long flights east, a doctor may suggest a different plan.

questions.q: What is a common rough guide for jet lag after flying east?

options.text: About one hour in total, whatever the distance
About one week, whatever the distance
About one day per time zone crossed

questions.explain: A common rough guide: jet lag lasts about a day per time zone after flying east and about half a day per time zone after flying west.

questions.q: What is a sensible first session at a new ground?

options.text: A few easy targets to see the new background
A full competition round, to test yourself
No shooting at all until the jet lag has gone

questions.explain: Easy targets first let you see how targets look against the new background and light.

questions.q: After a flight a few time zones west, what helps the body clock adjust?

options.text: Local time from day one, light in the evening
Bright light early in the morning, dim evenings
Long daytime naps and coffee late in the evening

questions.explain: After flying west the body clock has to move later: live on local time from the first day, get light in the late afternoon and evening, and avoid bright morning light. After flying east it is the other way round.

questions.q: How can you drink water at the ground?

options.text: In small sips through the day
Only when you are very thirsty
A lot at once, in the evening

questions.explain: Small, regular sips help you avoid the fluid loss that affects attention.

questions.q: How much coffee on competition day?

options.text: A large extra dose for focus
Your usual amount, not late in the day
None at all, because caffeine is prohibited

questions.explain: Keep your habit: a large dose can make the hands less steady, and caffeine is not prohibited.

questions.q: Why wash your hands before a snack at the ground?

options.text: Because the referee requires it
So that the gun does not slip in your hands
They may carry lead from cartridges

questions.explain: Lead often reaches the body through dirty hands and food.

questions.q: What can you do between stands on a long day?

options.text: Rest: talk, drink, find shade
Add up your score again and again
Stay on your phone all break

questions.explain: A tired head aims less well; resting between stands helps you switch on again for the next one.

questions.q: When may you drink alcohol on a shooting day?

options.text: At lunch, between two rounds
Before the first round, for a little courage
After shooting, if you don't shoot tomorrow

questions.explain: No alcohol before or during shooting, and none in the evening before another shooting day.

questions.q: When can you go to bed the night before?

options.text: At your usual time
Much earlier than usual
Late, after a long dinner

questions.explain: A usual bedtime with a 7–9 hour sleep window is a good default; going to bed much earlier often means lying awake.

questions.q: During a competition round the coach asks you to tell the shooter “more lead on the crosser”. What do you do?

options.text: Whisper it quickly while he loads
Pass it on after the next target
Decline politely: that would be coaching
Ask the referee to pass it on

questions.explain: Coaching during competition is forbidden and the shooter would get a yellow card. The rules do not say whether relaying advice is allowed, so stay on the safe side.

questions.q: What do the FITASC rulebooks say about interpreters?

options.text: They may stand on the stand
They need a referee’s licence
They count as coaches
Nothing: it is an open question

questions.explain: The rulebooks do not mention interpreters, so their exact position in competition is an open question for FITASC.

questions.q: In training, the coach says “Not bad, but you stopped the gun.” How do you translate?

options.text: Fully and in the same tone, both parts
Only the praise, to keep the guest happy
Only the fault, to save time
Add your own tip on how to fix it

questions.explain: You neither soften nor inflate: the whole message, in the coach’s tone, with nothing of your own.

questions.q: A coach and a shooter share no language. What helps most in the first session?

options.text: Long explanations, spoken slowly
Shooting more targets in silence
Agreed anchor words and hand signals
A translation app during the routine

questions.explain: A small agreed vocabulary and the coach’s signals carry most of a session; long explanations and phones during the routine get in the way.

questions.q: At a competition, the shooter’s coach asks the interpreter to pass on a tip. What is the safe practice?

options.text: Pass it on quietly between targets
Pass it on with the referee’s nod
Pass it on only between stands
Decline: pass on only official words

questions.explain: Coaching during the competition is forbidden, and the rules do not mention interpreters. Passing on only the referee, the jury and the organiser protects the shooter.

questions.q: When should the coach and the interpreter talk to the shooter on the stand?

options.text: While the shooter mounts
Just before the call
During the swing
When the gun is open

questions.explain: The shooter’s routine ends with the shot, and by the time the gun is closed it is well under way; words during it break the shooter’s focus.

questions.q: What will a shooter buy on a ClayAway tour?

options.text: Only the flight to the venue
One package: training, stay, transfers, programme
Only the targets and the cartridges

questions.explain: ClayAway is planned to bundle the main parts of the trip into one package.

questions.q: Who will be able to organise a ClayAway tour?

options.text: A coach, manager, club, ground or agency
Only the coach who leads the training
Only FITASC or a national federation

questions.explain: Organiser and coach are different roles, although a coach can organise a tour too.

questions.q: At a FITASC competition, may the tour coach give you tips on the stand?

options.text: Yes, because it is part of the package
Yes, if the referee does not object
No, coaching during the competition is not allowed

questions.explain: Under the FITASC rules the coach works with you before and after the competition, but not during it.

questions.q: In which time will a ClayAway tour programme be given?

options.text: In each participant's home time
In the venue's time zone, with the zone labelled
Without any times, only the dates

questions.explain: The programme is in local time, so that the schedule is not confused after the flight.
